question: For each of the 50 states: when a U.S. Senate seat falls vacant (death or resignation), may the governor appoint a temporary senator under the Seventeenth Amendment? If so, within what time, and must the appointee be of the departed senator's party (or be chosen from a list the party submits)? When is the special election held (the next regular general election, a date the governor sets, or within a fixed number of days), and is there a cutoff before a regular election after which the seat waits for it? Give the statutory citation for each state.
requestedBy: Empty offices and term dates thread

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: The game now fills a vacant Senate seat by a blanket rule: the governor appoints a drawn person of the departed senator's party ten days after the vacancy, and a special election at the next regular November congressional election chooses who serves the rest of the term. Whether each state allows the appointment, its party requirement and its special-election timing are not compiled.

sourcesChecked.source: Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-855, in the Mississippi Secretary of State's 2017 election code compilation (https://www.sos.ms.gov/sites/default/files/elections/MSCODE_Elections.pdf, PDF page 519)
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: The 2017 text requires the governor to issue a proclamation within 10 days and to hold an election within 90 days when more than 12 months remain in the term, and it allows a temporary appointment under stated conditions. It is a dated baseline: whether the section has been amended since 2017 is not verified. 2025 Senate Bill 2637 would change this procedure but is known only as an introduced bill; whether it or any later act was enacted is not settled. The game does not compile Mississippi's rule until the current text is confirmed.

terms.notice: 17 USC105 government works; statistics/facts only, not third-party content or logos.

title: How each state fills a vacant U.S. Senate seat
usableAnswer: A table with one row per state: appointment allowed (yes or no), deadline, party requirement, special-election timing rule and cutoff, and the citation.
whyItMatters: A playthrough set in Detroit found Michigan's Class I seat vacant from September 2033 with no appointment or special election, and eight Senate seats vacant nationally. The game now fills them by a stand-in rule until this is answered. Observer lives also found Mississippi's seat vacant from October 2041, and South Carolina's and Nevada's seats vacant for years.

findings.finding: Exact federal/DC rules and locked primary state facts are supplied where verified. Remaining state/local structure and age/tenure distributions are explicitly unresolved. Neither a legal age minimum nor town population implies a uniform age window or council size. No real-person names collected.
